audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim in Junod 1907 sec. 23 (pp. 11-12), now saved locally (no file was held before). Deciding source is a 1907 missionary elementary grammar, not the best available description, but every source opened agrees on penultimate prominence: Ouwehand 1965 pp. 11-12 ('accent... on the last syllable but one'), Junod sec. 2 (penultimate vowel long and accented), Selkirk 2011 after Kisseberth 1994 (all and only clause-penultimate vowels long, no lexical length), Lee & Riedel 2022 (instrumental; PL marks right edge of prosodic word/phonological phrase/IP, longest IP-finally, word-level PL not systematically established). Junod's final-accent exceptions (locative, imperative) follow from his apocopated 1907 spellings (-en, -n for modern -eni, -ani) and do not disturb 'fixed-dominant penultimate' (strict=false). Nothing suggests the kind/rule is wrong; what

sources.citation: Junod 1907, Elementary Grammar of the Thonga-Shangaan Language, sec. 23, archive.org djvu text of elementarygramma00juno
sources.quote: The accent is well marked. It falls on the penultimate, when the word is polysyllabic (except in the locative case and the imperative mood where it falls on the last syllable). Monosyllabic words have generally no accent.

sources.citation: Ouwehand, M. 1965. Everyday Tsonga. Johannesburg: Central Mission Press / Swiss Mission. 124 pp. (archive.org m-ouwehand-everyday-tsonga)
sources.quote: 'Usually the accent in the word is on the last syllable but one (the penultimate).' No locative/imperative exception mentioned; p.79 fn: tata wavo 'pronounced with the stress on vo (with a long vowel), this being considered the short form of vona'.
sources.locator: Introduction, D. 'Accentuation and Intonation', pp. 11-12 (djvu l.477-484); footnote p. 79

sources.quote: 'The accent is well marked. It falls on the penultimate, when the word is polysyllabic (except in the locative case and the imperative mood where it falls on the last syllable). Monosyllabic words have generally no accent.' Sec. 2: vowel 'generally long in the penultimate ... on which the accent generally falls.'

sources.citation: Lee, Seunghun J. & Kristina Riedel. 2022. Pre-nominal DP modifiers and penultimate lengthening in Xitsonga. Stellenbosch Papers in Linguistics Plus 62: 107-134. doi:10.5842/62-0-907
sources.quote: 'Prosodically, PL ... marks the right edge of a prosodic level in Xitsonga at the levels of the prosodic word, phonological phrase, or intonational phrase.' fn.1: 'No systematic study reports word-level PL in Xitsonga.' Sec. 4: 'PL in Xitsonga is reported to mark the boundary of an intonational phrase (Kisseberth 1994, Selkirk 2011). Whether or not penultimate syllables of the lower prosodic levels ... are also realised as lengthened vowels has not been reported. Anecdotally ... PL is heard at the prosodic word level.' Instrumental (Praat durations, multiple speakers).

sources.quote: 'In Xitsonga, all and only vowels that are penultimate in the clause are long (V:). There is no lexical vowel length contrast; this penultimate lengthening is introduced by the phonology.' Secondary (relays Kisseberth 1994).
